scores.accuracy_concern: Cohen-Mansfield and Taylor 2004 is one US nursing home sample over 20 years old; check the 69% and 86% denominators in the full text and present it as dated US data; the five-point daily check needs a sourced audiology leaflet.
scores.sharpen: Anchor it in a UK care home source (for example the RNID care home work) and make the record change concrete: 'aid worked this morning: yes/no' beside 'hearing aid: yes'.

scores.accuracy_concern: The NICE NG98 follow-up timing (6 to 12 weeks) must be checked in the guideline text, and the McCormack and Fortnum review must be confirmed in PubMed before any non-use figure is given.
scores.sharpen: Give one verified figure on how many people stop wearing new aids, so the settling-in advice has a reason attached, and keep the question card as the visual.

scores.accuracy_concern: A council assessment and vision rehabilitation can be requested without certification, so the post should not imply the certificate is the only route; the CVI process and concessions differ between England and Scotland.
scores.sharpen: Say plainly that you can also ask the council for a sensory or vision rehabilitation assessment directly, and write separate England and Scotland lines.

scores.accuracy_concern: Cat-PROM5 is a research and audit tool, not something clinics routinely use to decide on referral; do not imply that it is.
scores.sharpen: Merge its glare, dim-light and contrast detail into C14-13 rather than running a second post on why the letter chart is not enough.

scores.accuracy_concern: The trials were in adults with mild to moderate loss, not specifically older people; check the age range in the 2026 review before addressing older readers, and explain that 'large' refers to a standardised effect size.
scores.sharpen: Lead with a concrete everyday gain (following talk at a family meal) and leave the memory result to C14-17 if both are used.

scores.accuracy_concern: Sumby and Pollack 1954 tested young listeners with normal hearing in noise; cite a study of older adults with hearing loss for the benefit of seeing the face, and mark the typing advice as judgement.
scores.sharpen: Keep the two-panel patient's-eye view and add one sentence on masks and hands over the mouth so the post covers the other common way faces are hidden.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check the current version of the Accessible Information Standard (it was reviewed after 2017) and state that it applies in England only.
scores.sharpen: Add the equivalent route for readers in Scotland and one line on what to do if the flag is recorded but letters still arrive in small print.

scores.values_concern: Describe the partner's experience without presenting the person with hearing loss as a burden on the household.
scores.accuracy_concern: The 98% figure means at least one item of third-party disability, mostly mild, and must not read as nearly all spouses being badly affected; the ACE trial does not show that involving partners helps both people.
scores.sharpen: Drop the 98% headline figure and build the post on one practical joint tactic, supported by a study that included communication partners.

scores.accuracy_concern: Advice on glasses between operations varies by surgeon and prescription, so present removing or changing the lens on the operated side as one option to ask about; the Foss 2006 falls result was not statistically significant.
scores.sharpen: Find an NHS or RCOphth patient leaflet that states the between-eyes glasses advice, and make the pre-operative question the closing line.

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE NG98 says to be seen within 24 hours by ENT or an emergency department; match that wording rather than a same-day GP appointment, and keep the uncertain benefit of steroids stated.
scores.sharpen: Give the reader the exact sentence to say on the phone, and name ENT or the emergency department as the destination.

scores.accuracy_concern: Low vision aids improve reading in trials, but the Cochrane review found low-certainty evidence and no clear best device, so avoid 'restore'; instrumental activity scales (Lawton) do include finances and medicines, so name the Barthel specifically.
scores.sharpen: Add medicine labels and the privacy of bank letters to the visual, and close with the single assessment question to add.

scores.accuracy_concern: No trial shows that night lights alone reduce falls; the dark-adaptation and numb-feet reasoning is physiology, and 'leaves mainly the inner ear' oversimplifies balance.
scores.sharpen: Say more clearly how this differs from the earlier night-light advice (E072), open with the numb-feet case rather than a textbook line, and keep the claim to physiology.

scores.accuracy_concern: NICE NG77 says not to restrict access on visual acuity, but local criteria and waits vary; Harwood 2005 studied women over 70 only; give the complication rate from the NOD audit or leave it out.
scores.sharpen: Fold in the glare and dim-light examples from C14-04 so the reader knows what to describe at the optometrist, and say who the trial studied.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check the sighted guide description against RNIB or Guide Dogs text, and give the #hellomynameis campaign a checkable source.
scores.sharpen: Make porters, radiographers and transport staff the named readers, and cut the sight-loss prevalence claim unless a figure is verified.

scores.values_concern: Avoid any suggestion that families who were absent or silent at a death failed the person, and keep the tone free of false comfort.
scores.accuracy_concern: The EEG study was very small; check in the full text how many unresponsive patients showed each response ('most' may overstate it), and do not imply awareness or understanding.
scores.sharpen: Give the actual numbers of patients in the study, and end on the practical line about saying who you are and keeping a hearing aid in while comfortable.

scores.accuracy_concern: 'Fifteen' and 'fifty' differ mainly in the ending and stress rather than a single high-frequency consonant; use pairs that differ by s, f, th or sh, and source 'shouting distorts speech' to audiology guidance.
scores.sharpen: Swap in word pairs that clearly turn on high-pitched consonants and show the rephrasing example in the visual.

scores.accuracy_concern: The ARIC-cohort finding was a prespecified sensitivity analysis of a secondary kind, not the primary result; do not quote a percentage slowing as an effect.
scores.sharpen: Give clinicians one sentence they can use in place of the dementia argument when recommending hearing aids.

scores.values_concern: Criticise the gap between the NICE recommendation and provision without blaming GP practices, which are often not commissioned to provide it.
scores.accuracy_concern: The 'up to 57%' care home figure is an old estimate cited by AAO-HNS; the claim that many GP practices stopped wax removal needs a dated RNID or official source.
scores.sharpen: Add what a reader can do now (ask the practice where NHS wax removal is provided locally) so it gives an action as well as a criticism.

scores.accuracy_concern: Case reports show that it can happen, not how often; the tissue press and tear-duct occlusion lowered plasma levels, but clinical benefit is less certain; the Müller trial is 2020, and the press duration must come from the BNF or SPC.
scores.sharpen: Add one line on how to find the drops (ask directly, since eye drops are often missing from medicine lists), and name the non-beta-blocker alternatives in general terms.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check the '1 of 16' figure in Teunisse 1996; the 60 of 505 figure was from a visually impaired clinic population, not all people with sight loss.
scores.sharpen: Add one sentence telling eye clinics to mention Charles Bonnet syndrome at diagnosis of sight loss, which puts the position into action.

scores.accuracy_concern: The evidence is a review of case reports and series, so prevalence and treatment effects are uncertain; the opening puts ears before every other cause, but brain disease and medicines need assessment alongside.
scores.sharpen: Rephrase the opening so hearing assessment and medicine review come before antipsychotics rather than before 'anyone considers' other causes.

scores.accuracy_concern: The intervention included referral for cataract surgery and other treatment, not only new glasses; adaptation to new glasses is the authors' hypothesis, and 'a smaller prescription change' is an inference the trial did not test.
scores.sharpen: Put the Harwood cataract result beside it in the visual, so readers see that the type of vision correction made the difference, not vision correction itself.

scores.accuracy_concern: The 7% dual sensory figure is from a small sample (Dupuis 2015); use a population estimate or omit it, and confirm the deafblind guidance wording and its status under the Care Act.
scores.sharpen: Open with a concrete situation (a person who can no longer lip-read because of macular degeneration) and give the exact name of the assessment to ask for.

scores.accuracy_concern: Wavy lines from suspected wet macular degeneration need urgent referral, but the NICE NG82 timeframe may not be same day; check each symptom's recommended timeframe and pathway.
scores.sharpen: Group the symptoms by where to go (999, eye casualty, optometrist today) instead of one 'today' list.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check the BSR 2020 wording on time windows (ultrasound within about one week, biopsy within about two weeks of starting glucocorticoids) and on dosing for visual symptoms.
scores.sharpen: Make the older-person detail the angle: vague presentations (weight loss, tiredness, jaw ache) that delay suspicion, not only the treatment order.

scores.accuracy_concern: Oghalai 2000 was one US inner-city clinic sample, so 9% is not a general prevalence and the link with falls is cross-sectional.
scores.sharpen: Add a line on adapting the test (side-lying test or support) for people with neck or back problems, which makes it usable in frail older people.

scores.accuracy_concern: The comparison arm received targeted screening, not no screening; describe it as universal versus targeted screening, and mark the reasons for the null result as the authors' interpretation.
scores.sharpen: Name the one step most likely to fail (taking up the referral) and what a practice can do about it.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check that UK NHS audiology services use COSI or the Glasgow profile routinely before saying 'some services'.
scores.sharpen: Combine with C14-02 as one 'before and after your hearing appointment' post, or make the opening a situation rather than an instruction.

scores.accuracy_concern: Santos 2004 studied smell clinic patients, not the general older population; check the 37% and 19% figures; Doty 1984 is old and measured smell identification.
scores.sharpen: Lead with carbon monoxide, which nobody can smell, so the alarm advice holds whatever the reader's sense of smell.

scores.values_concern: Use 'Deaf BSL users' consistently and present BSL as a language, not a deficit.
scores.accuracy_concern: Emond 2015 was a convenience sample of Deaf BSL users of all ages; the link with poor access is an inference; check whether the NHS England interpreting guidance applies beyond primary care.
scores.sharpen: Strengthen the older-person angle with a sourced point about older Deaf people in care homes, or cut that line.

scores.accuracy_concern: Check the exact Dupuis 2015 finding on adjusted MoCA scores and that it applies to the MoCA only; the hearing-impaired MoCA source needs verifying.
scores.sharpen: Make 'record the adaptations with the score' the closing instruction, and make the difference from the earlier family-facing hearing and eyes post (E006) explicit.

scores.accuracy_concern: Evidence of cognitive or functional benefit from cataract surgery in established dementia is weak and observational; do not imply cognitive improvement, and the drop regimen and lying-still time need sourced figures.
scores.sharpen: Base the post on the planning questions and the principle of not excluding people because of the diagnosis, and drop the cognitive-benefit claim.

allocation_reason: All 32 candidates score 36 or more with no disqualifying flag (27 still clear the bar if it is rescaled for the formula's true maximum of 55), and the top 14 cover hearing, vision, smell and balance for both audiences without duplication.
balance_note: The top 14 split 7 practitioner, 6 public and 1 both, which is balanced. Series are spread across Teaching round, Reading the evidence, Small detail, Ask this, What gets counted and Weighing it up, but none is from Who gets left out or Care that works. Three of the top 14 are about cataract or glasses (C14-22, C14-09, C14-13). Consider swapping one of them for C14-30 (Deaf BSL users) or C14-03 (sight loss certification for people living alone) to cover exclusion, and C14-29 (smell) would widen the senses covered. C14-15, C14-26 and C14-19 overlap the palliative, falls and medicines categories, so check they are not also picked there.
